title: Securing the Power Query connector ecosystem in Fabric
summary: Microsoft describes a strategic shift to bring Power Query's data connectors fully in-house, lays out a four-stage connector lifecycle (Preview, GA, Transparent Migration, Retirement) meant to make upgrades predictable, and lists several V2 connectors (Snowflake, Google BigQuery, Vertica, IBM Netezza, Amazon Redshift) that reached general availability under this approach.
audience: Power BI/Fabric data engineers and platform admins who depend on third-party source connectors (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Netezza, Vertica) and need to plan around Microsoft's connector versioning, migration, and retirement policy.
why_it_matters: Connector supply-chain security and lifecycle predictability directly affect production dataflows and semantic models built on third-party sources; knowing that legacy connector versions get retired only after a supported migration path exists (rather than abruptly) shapes how teams schedule connector upgrades and vendor risk reviews.
takeaways: Microsoft is moving toward building and maintaining all Power Query connectors in-house rather than relying on third-party-maintained connector code, framed as a supply-chain security investment.
Connectors now follow a four-stage lifecycle: Preview, General Availability, Transparent Migration, and Retirement.
Several V2 (Microsoft-owned, ADBC-based for Snowflake) connectors reached GA around September 2025: Snowflake, Google BigQuery, and Amazon Redshift.
Vertica and IBM Netezza gained a 'Bring Your Own Driver' model via the on-premises data gateway (OPDG) instead of a Microsoft-shipped V2 connector.
Legacy connector versions are retired only once a transparently migrated, more secure alternative is broadly available, not on an arbitrary deadline.

claims.text: Microsoft states it is bringing all Power Query connectors in-house, positioning Microsoft-owned connector development and maintenance as a deliberate reduction of long-term security and operational supply-chain risk compared to externally maintained connector code.

Microsoft describes a structured four-stage connector lifecycle: Preview (early access for evaluation), General Availability (fully supported, production-ready with ongoing updates/versioning), Transparent Migration (supported transition as implementations change, e.g. new security models or protocols), and Retirement (legacy versions removed once a more secure alternative is broadly available).

Retirement of a legacy connector version happens only after a transparently migrated, more secure and reliable replacement is broadly available, rather than on a fixed calendar deadline independent of migration readiness.

The Snowflake V2 Power Query connector, which reached general availability, is built on ADBC (Arrow Database Connectivity) and is described as the foundation for Microsoft's modern, in-house connectivity approach going forward.
A fully supported Google BigQuery V2 connector reached general availability following what Microsoft describes as a multi-semester investment in stability, performance, and enterprise readiness.

An Amazon Redshift V2 connector reached general availability, developed with Amazon Redshift's collaboration as part of Microsoft's strategy for consistent, secure connectivity across major cloud data warehouses.

Vertica and IBM Netezza connectivity instead uses a 'Bring Your Own Driver' model through the on-premises data gateway (OPDG), letting customers supply their own driver for these sources rather than Microsoft shipping and maintaining a V2 connector directly.

Microsoft frames these V2 connector releases (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, and the Vertica/Netezza Bring Your Own Driver model) as reaching general availability around September 2025, ahead of this post's publication, as part of the broader connector modernization push.
Microsoft positions customer-submitted Fabric Ideas as a direct input into which connectors get built or improved next and into roadmap prioritization for the Power Query connector portfolio.
